key_insight: RL-trained LLM agents can learn spurious tool-use rules, triggering tools from superficial prompt cues instead of real task need.
engineering_relevance: For reliable agentic systems, tool policies should be rewarded for necessity, not just success, to reduce brittle cue-driven behavior.
method: Built controlled synthetic QA and math environments with injected tool-correlated but causally irrelevant cues.
Compared standard RL-trained tool-selection against counterfactual settings where cues stayed but tools were not needed.
Added a dense decision-level reward using an LLM judge to score whether each tool call was necessary.
evidence_signal: Across counterfactual evaluations, spurious tool invocation rose by up to 39% when cues were present without tool necessity, and the failure appeared mainly after the agent had already learned the tool well.
watch_item: An LLM-judge reward may be sensitive to judge quality and criteria, so deployment needs careful calibration to avoid new bias or reward gaming.
paper_title: Spurious Tool Use: When RL Agents Learn the Wrong Reason to Act
